judgments.reasoning_cat1: The operative measure of damages is "the Shipper's replacement value applicable to the kind and quantity of Commodities so lost, damaged or destroyed." "Replacement value" is nowhere defined and is fairly susceptible of at least two constructions: the Shipper's cost to replace the goods (manufacturing/acquisition cost) or the value at which the goods would be replaced in the market (invoice/sales price, including margin). The internal drafting makes the ambiguity worse, not better: sentence one fixes the measure as "replacement value," but sentence two then directs deduction of salvage "from the invoice price" — a different metric introduced without definition or reconciliation, implying the parties may have meant invoice price all along. The third sentence ("some of the Commodities may be disposed of in a manner that will prevent the damaged goods from being sold on the open market") adds a further undefined qualifier bearing on salvage. Also unclear is why "Customer shall deduct" salvage when the loss measure is the Shipper's, a non-party. This is the profile of the "premises/person/occupy" clause in example 1_1: undefined ordinary-language terms doing dispositive work, each reasonably bearing more than one meaning. High probability of intrinsic ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 9(a) (liability trigger and excepted causes), § 9(c) (49 C.F.R. Part 370 claims procedure, with the delay-indemnity sentence struck through), § 10(d) (cargo insurance of $100,000 per vehicle, with "not less than" struck out), and § 10's closing sentence ("The insurance required under this Section 10 does not limit Carrier's liability under the provisions of Sections 8 and 9"). There is real friction: 9(b) imposes an uncapped replacement-value measure while the negotiated cargo insurance was struck down to a fixed $100,000 per vehicle, and § 10's non-limitation sentence must be read to leave the carrier exposed far beyond its required coverage — harmonisable, but the hand-alteration of 10(d) signals the parties bargained about a cap that 9(b) does not reflect. § 9(c)'s incorporation of Part 370 (which contemplates the Carmack "actual loss or injury" measure) also sits uneasily with a contractual replacement-value measure. These are reconcilable with effort, so below the flag line, but materially elevated.
judgments.clause_name: Liabilities and Claims for Commodities, para 9(b) (measure of loss — "replacement value")

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard recital block. It defines "Commodities," "Shipper," and "Services" and identifies the parties. Minor scrivener's slips ("Southern Refrigerated Transport Arkansas corporation" omits "an"; "beverages alcoholic in nature" appears later) do not create competing reasonable meanings. Nothing dispositive turns on an undefined term here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The recital says Carrier is engaged in transporting property "as a contract carrier," but § 3's operative sentence reads "Broker agrees to provide the Services," and § 6(c) refers to "any prior contract ... which purported to be a contract Broker agreement," while § 10 refers to "an insurance Broker." That is a recital-vs-operative mismatch of the type the taxonomy describes, but "Broker" is a transparent find-and-replace artifact in a two-party agreement whose only defined parties are Carrier and Customer, so a court would treat it as an obvious scrivener's error rather than a genuine incoherence. Mildly elevated only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "shall continue for a period of one year from the date of execution or unless earlier terminated" contains a stray "or" before "unless," but the sense is plain and the 30-day notice mechanic, the year-to-year extension, and the post-termination delivery obligation are all definite. No term carries two reasonable meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The cover page states "Effective Date: January 1, 2008," while § 1 says the Agreement "shall be effective upon its execution"; the signature blocks are dated 12/26/07 (Carrier) and 2 Jan 08 (Customer). Those three dates do not line up, and the term, the year-to-year renewal, and the § 22 audit window all run from the effective date. Checked § 16 (Default), which permits termination after a 30-day cure — consistent with, not contradictory to, § 1's without-cause right. Elevated for the date mismatch but short of a genuine conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three short declarative sentences. "Non-exclusive basis" is a term of art with a settled meaning, and the two illustrative sentences confirm it in both directions. Nothing vague or double-edged.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 3 (Scope of Work) and § 15 (Assignment; Subsidiaries and Divisions). Nothing anywhere commits volume to Carrier or restricts Carrier's other business, so the non-exclusivity statement sits consistently with the whole instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Several nameable soft spots. (i) The operative lead-in says "Broker agrees to provide the Services" in an agreement whose only defined parties are Carrier and Customer — the promisor is misidentified. (ii) Subsection (e) is a textbook general-vs-specific problem: "Special services such as, picking up and delivering freight on short notice, weekend services, twenty-four hour services, holiday service and other similar services shall be provided" — the catch-all "other similar services" sits against enumerated specifics with no boundary and no pricing, inviting ejusdem generis dispute. (iii) "suitable equipment," "satisfactory and legal manner," "good appearance," and the "desire and capability to pursue EDI opportunities" are standards without an ascertainable boundary. (iv) The lettering skips (g). Enough named textual defects to sit near the line, though most of the section is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsection (m) defines "delivery" as transport "to consignee's door or job site," while Exhibit A Item 200.1 defines the same term as transport "to consignee's receiving location from the Shipper's facilities" — two operative definitions of one defined term, and § 24's last sentence makes the Exhibit control, so the body's definition is displaced by its own contract. Subsection (c) conditions non-exclusive/commingled use on "Customer's prior written consent," whereas Exhibit A Item 140 conditions it on "a written request for non-exclusive use ... provided to Carrier by Shipper" — a different consenting party. Subsection (e) promises weekend/24-hour/holiday service while Item 190 limits included rates to "business hours." Real, if minor, friction; short of an irreconcilable conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite and conventional. "Prima facie evidence" is a settled legal standard, the noting exception is expressly stated, and the required contents of the delivery receipt are enumerated. No term bears competing meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its subordination rule ("in the event of a conflict, this Agreement shall govern") tracks § 22's first paragraph exactly, and the delivery-receipt requirement supports the § 9 claims machinery and § 6(d) billing documentation. Checked § 22 and § 24 — no inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Notification and authorization duties are stated with definite triggers and channels. "Prior to Carrier accepting legal responsibility for the shipment" is the only loose phrase, and § 9(a) supplies the answer (custody, possession or control). Not genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsections (c) and (d) defer to Exhibit A; Item 220 (Re-consignments) and Item 230 (Return of shipments) do exist and cover those topics, so the cross-references land. Item 230's own rate is indeterminate, but that is Item 230's defect, not this clause's. Consistent with § 5's own notice mechanics and § 3(f).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Mostly hard numbers (30 days to pay, 180 days to present, 60 days' notice of proposed rate changes). Two soft spots: 6(c) refers to "any prior contract between them which purported to be a contract Broker agreement" (wrong party label again), and 6(d)'s "all transportation charges due on any such shipment shall be cancelled by Carrier" states a forfeiture in an odd voice. Neither creates a genuine choice between two reasonable meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 24, whose last sentence makes the Exhibits control over the Agreement in a conflict, against 6(c)'s "Except as otherwise provided herein, the rates ... set forth in Exhibit A ... shall be the sole rates" and 6(e)'s mutual-consent requirement — a mild circularity about which document wins, but the practical result is the same. Also checked § 24's supersession sentence against 6(c)'s ratification of "all acts performed ... pursuant to any prior contract": ratifying past performance is not the same as keeping a prior agreement alive, so no true conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Fully quantified: 180 days to bill, 180 days to contest, 18 months to sue, prevailing-party fee shifting. "Prevailing party" is a familiar, judicially administrable standard. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 9(e), which sets a different limitations period (two years and a day) — but that runs on cargo claims from written disallowance, while § 7 governs undercharge/overcharge actions on freight charges. Different subject matter, so the two periods coexist rather than conflict. No other limitations or fee provision in the instrument.
judgments.clause_name: 7. Limitation on Actions for Charges and Fees

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional broad-form indemnity. "Arising out of or resulting from the performance of the Services" is settled indemnity language, the parenthetical carve-outs (Customer's property in, Commodities out) are express, and the negligence exception is doubly bounded ("except to the extent (but only to the extent)"). No named term is doubly reasonable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The express exclusion of "the Commodities" from this indemnity cleanly hands cargo loss to § 9, avoiding overlap. Checked § 10's closing sentence, which confirms insurance does not cap liability under §§ 8 and 9 — the sections are drafted to interlock. Also checked § 17's tax indemnity: separate subject matter.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Grammatically mangled ("all underlying carrier's Carrier utilizes has received"), but the standard invoked is an external, binary DOT rating — "Satisfactory" versus "Conditional" or "Unsatisfactory" — which is objectively verifiable. The clause is definite in substance despite the syntax.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 15, which bars assignment or transfer of the Agreement without consent, against this section's (and §§ 8, 9(a), 12(a)'s) repeated assumption that Carrier will use "underlying carriers." Subcontracting is not assignment, so this is tension rather than contradiction, and no provision anywhere authorizes or conditions subcontracting. Mildly elevated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Obligations are tied to identified external legal standards (D.O.T., E.P.A., F.D.A., the Sanitary Food Transportation Act of 1990) and to enumerated notification triggers. "Including but not limited to" precedes examples of a duty already stated at full breadth ("all ... applicable" laws), so the catch-all adds nothing uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Reinforces § 3(a) (licences and permits), § 3(b)–(c) (commingling), and § 11 (safety rating) without contradicting any of them. Checked § 13's notice mechanics — the prompt-notification duty here is consistent with them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Named delivery methods, a named fax-plus-hardcopy protocol, and specific addresses and attention parties. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: § 13 opens "All notices and amendments shall be in writing," yet § 5(b), § 6(c) and Exhibit A Item 200.9 all direct notification "by telephone or facsimile," and Item 200.6 requires immediate notification without specifying a channel. Read strictly, telephone notice would not satisfy § 13. Harmonisable by reading § 13 as governing formal contractual notices and the operational provisions as governing day-to-day communication, so below the flag line, but a real seam.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: identified categories (indemnities, warranties, guarantees, obligations) survive expiration, termination or cancellation and bind successors and assigns. One-sidedness (only Carrier's obligations survive) is a bargaining outcome, not an ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 1's final sentence, which preserves "any obligation accruing before such termination" for either party — broader as to parties, narrower as to timing. The two overlap without contradicting. Also checked § 15/§ 23, which likewise bind successors and assigns; consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The stray conjunction is a genuine defect: "Neither Customer or Carrier shall assign or transfer this Agreement in whole or in part or without the prior written consent of the other party." As written, the consent proviso is joined disjunctively to the prohibition, so the sentence is fairly readable either as an absolute bar on any assignment, whole or partial, plus a separate bar on assigning without consent, or as the intended "in whole or in part without the prior written consent." That is a nameable ambiguity in the operative prohibition, not merely bad grammar. Held below the flag line because the second reading is overwhelmingly the natural one.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 23 (Assignability of Contract), which contemplates "the transfer or assignment from Customer to their underlying Shipper" and says the terms are unaffected by it — presupposing an assignment that § 15 would require Carrier's written consent to make. Two separate assignment sections pointing different directions is untidy, though § 23 can be read as addressing only the consequences of a permitted assignment. Elevated, not flagged.
judgments.clause_name: 15. Assignment of Agreement; Subsidiaries and Divisions

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single definite sentence: written request, 30-day cure, then termination. "Default" is undefined but takes its ordinary meaning as breach of the stated obligations; no competing reasonable construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 1, which already lets either party terminate without cause on 30 days' notice, making this cure-and-terminate right largely redundant — a party could bypass the cure period entirely under § 1. Redundancy and a weakened cure right, but the two operate on the same 30-day clock and do not contradict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard independent-contractor recital with an enumerated tax and benefits indemnity. "Exclusive control and direction" is the settled formulation. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with § 8 (general indemnity, different subject matter), § 3(d) (Carrier supplies drivers) and § 10(c) (Carrier carries workers' compensation). Nothing in the instrument gives Customer direction over Carrier's personnel that would undercut the status.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate severability with an express statement of the parties' counterfactual intent. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Operates on every other provision without displacing any. No provision anywhere makes a term non-severable or conditions the agreement on the validity of a particular clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A general-vs-specific issue is present: after four enumerated categories ("costs, pricing information, procedures, computer software systems") the clause sweeps in "and other details of Customer's business," a catch-all whose reach against the specifics is exactly the ejusdem generis / expressio unius problem the taxonomy describes. There is also no duration, no carve-out for publicly available or independently developed information, and no marking requirement, so the boundary of what is confidential is left open. Elevated but not flagged — one-way confidentiality of this breadth is common and courts routinely enforce it as written.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 14 (Survivability), which carries Carrier's obligations past termination and so supplies the missing duration; and § 22, which grants Customer audit access to Carrier's records without a reciprocal confidentiality duty — asymmetric but not contradictory. No provision requires Carrier to disclose the protected information to a third party.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The nameable problem is the disjunction: the Agreement is governed by "THE APPLICABLE LAWS OF THE UNITED STATES OR THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF OHIO," with no rule for choosing between them and no party given the election. Read one way it is a redundant nod to federal preemption (Carmack, 49 U.S.C.) with Ohio law filling the gaps; read another it is an unresolved alternative. The venue half is by contrast fully definite (S.D. Ohio and Ohio state courts). The preemption reading is the natural one, so this stays below the flag line.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 9(c) (49 C.F.R. Part 370) and § 6(f) (49 C.F.R. Part 378) — both incorporate federal regulation, which supports rather than undermines the "federal where applicable, Ohio otherwise" reading. Party residences (Arkansas Carrier; Customer described as a Massachusetts corporation with a Pennsylvania notice address) do not conflict with an Ohio forum selection.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Narrow and self-limiting: excuse is confined to "Acts of God or circumstances and/or conditions occurring without human intervention" that no reasonable foresight could have prevented, with payment obligations expressly carved out. "Without human intervention" is unusual but is a boundary, not a vagueness — it excludes strikes, war and government action. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked § 9(a), which excuses cargo liability for "acts of God, the public enemy or public authority" — two of those three plainly involve human intervention and so fall outside § 21's excuse. The provisions govern different obligations (cargo liability versus performance generally), so a court can give each effect, but the two excuse lists are drawn on inconsistent principles. Mildly elevated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three definite paragraphs: subordination of shipping documents, primacy over prior contracts and tariffs, and a two-year post-termination audit right. The only loose thread is "for a period of two years after such termination," where "such termination" has no antecedent (the sentence speaks of "the term of this Agreement"), but the intended referent is obvious.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph two says the Agreement and its Exhibits "will be the sole provisions governing the Services" and resolves any tariff conflict "in favor of the provisions set forth herein," while § 24's final sentence resolves Agreement-versus-Exhibit conflicts in favour of the Exhibits. Those are different conflicts (external documents versus internal hierarchy), so they are reconcilable, but the instrument states its priority rules in two places using opposite defaults. Also checked § 4, whose bill-of-lading subordination rule duplicates paragraph one exactly.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The transfer or assignment from Customer to their underlying Shipper" is loosely drawn — it is unclear what is transferred (the Agreement, the claim, the freight charges) and "their" has an uncertain referent — and "shall not be affected, modified, altered, or changed in any respect" is a piled-up formulation. Still, the operative point (a Customer-to-Shipper transfer does not alter the terms) is intelligible. Below the line.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This section contemplates a transfer or assignment from Customer to the underlying Shipper as something that may simply happen, while § 15 provides that neither party "shall assign or transfer this Agreement in whole or in part" without the other's prior written consent. Having two separately captioned assignment sections (§ 15 and § 23) with different premises is the sort of whole-instrument untidiness that generates disputes, though § 23 can be harmonised as addressing only the effect of a transfer that § 15 has permitted. Elevated, not flagged.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional integration and supersession clause; each sentence is definite, and the priority rule in the last sentence is stated without hedging. No term bears competing meanings on its own wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The last sentence inverts the usual hierarchy: "If any provisions of the Exhibits and Schedules thereto are in conflict with the Agreement, the provisions of the Exhibits and Schedules shall control." That has live consequences elsewhere — it makes Exhibit A Item 200.1's definition of "delivery" override § 3(m)'s different definition, and Item 140's Shipper-request mechanism override § 3(c)'s Customer-consent requirement. It also sits against § 22's repeated insistence that "the terms, conditions and provisions of this Agreement shall govern" and that tariff conflicts resolve "in favor of the provisions set forth herein," and against § 6(c)'s "Except as otherwise provided herein." The instrument therefore states its own precedence in more than one direction. Reconcilable (§ 22 addresses external documents), but this is the provision that activates the Exhibit-versus-body mismatches, so materially elevated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short, definite statements: no charge for arranging or fulfilling appointments, and phone or fax scheduling permitted. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates § 3(k) word for word and matches Schedule B's "No charge" entry for Item 100. Also consistent with § 5(a)'s appointment-making duty. Fully aligned.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: There is a genuine internal tension between the two numbered paragraphs on how detention is computed: paragraph 1 sets "$65.00 per hour or fraction thereof in excess of the two hours," which bills a partial hour as a full hour, while paragraph 2 says "$/hour paid in 15 minute increments," which bills to the quarter-hour. On a 20-minute overage those produce $65 and about $21.67 respectively. The naming is precise elsewhere (two-hour free period, $390 cap, exclusion of early/late arrival differentials), so this is a discrete measurement ambiguity rather than pervasive vagueness. Elevated but short of the flag.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked Schedule B ("$65 per Hour, maximum $390"), which matches paragraph 1 and is silent on increments, and Exhibit A Item 200.10 ("2 hours free time for unloading with power"), which matches the free period exactly. Item 260 waives detention for drop trailers, a distinct no-power scenario. No cross-provision conflict.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 120 – Detention With Power

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite: the trigger (Carrier required by Shipper to sign for and hold a trailer), a two-business-day free period with the weekdays enumerated, $40.00 per day, and an express carve-out for the first Saturday and Sunday. "May be assessed" is permissive rather than uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Matches Schedule B ($40 per Day). Checked Item 320 (Intermodal Storage, $100 per day) — different scope, expressly limited to intermodal and keyed to Item 310's free-time schedule, so the two storage rates do not collide. Also checked Item 260, which waives demurrage on drop trailers at consignor facilities; this item covers Carrier holding a signed-for trailer, a different situation.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 130 – Storage – OTR Shipments

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, definite: exclusive use of the trailer is the default entitlement for every tendered load, displaced only by a written request for non-exclusive use. The trigger, the form (written), and the exception are all specified.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The consenting party does not match the body of the Agreement. § 3(c) provides that for TL movements Carrier shall not commingle "without Customer's prior written consent," whereas this Item lets the exception be triggered by "a written request for non-exclusive use ... provided to Carrier by Shipper" — and Shipper is a third party to this contract, not the counterparty. Because § 24 makes the Exhibits control in a conflict, the Exhibit's Shipper-request mechanism would displace Customer's own consent right. Real friction, though a court could harmonise by treating Shipper as acting through Customer under the § 3 framework. Elevated; just below the flag.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 140 – Exclusive Use of Vehicle

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Fully quantified: the trigger (consignee requires carrier personnel to sort and segregate), the rate ($0.30 per hundred pounds), a $50.00 per-stop minimum and a $125 per-shipment maximum. Nothing open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Matches Schedule B exactly ($0.30 per hundredweight, min $50 per stop, max $125 per shipment). Checked § 6(d), which requires unloading/lumping receipts to support such billing, and Item 290 (Lumper Charges), which covers hired laborers rather than carrier personnel — complementary, not overlapping. § 3(l) assigns loading to Customer's employees, a different operation.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 170 – Labor - Driver Loading or Unloading

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The two numbered paragraphs state different triggers for the same charge. Paragraph 1 conditions layover on the truck and driver being "detained overnight"; paragraph 2 describes the charge as a "[r]ate per day for detention in excess of six hours." A six-hour daytime detention satisfies paragraph 2 but not paragraph 1, so it is genuinely uncertain when the charge attaches. Compounding this, paragraph 2 states no figure at all ("Rate per day" with the amount omitted), leaving the item's own text incomplete. This is the strongest intrinsic defect among the Exhibit A items, though a court would likely read paragraph 1's overnight requirement as controlling and take the rate from Schedule B.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B supplies the missing amount ($390 per day), which cures the blank but not the trigger mismatch. Checked Item 120 (Detention with Power), whose $390 maximum is the same figure as one layover day — so on a long same-day detention it is unclear whether the $390 detention cap or a $390 layover day applies, and whether both could be billed. Overlapping charges without a stated boundary between them, but each is separately administrable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "During business hours" is undefined and is the only term doing limiting work in the sentence — for a 24-hour trucking operation with no stated hours for consignees or shippers, its boundary is uncertain. The rest (one pick up, one delivery or tender, one site, placement of vehicle at the designated loading and unloading sites) is definite. Elevated slightly for the undefined "business hours."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: § 3(e) requires Carrier to provide "weekend services, twenty-four hour services, holiday service," while this Item confines the included service to business hours and Schedule B prices Item 190 at "No charge" — so it is unclear whether after-hours service is free (per § 3(e), unpriced anywhere) or outside the base rate (per this Item). § 6(c) then forbids any accessorial not approved in advance. Also duplicative of Item 200.1, which states the same one-pickup/one-delivery inclusion in different words. Genuine but modest tension.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 190 – Pick Up or Delivery

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Several nameable defects in one item. Paragraph 3 is syntactically broken — "Carrier certifies that no trailer is used for the transportation of Shipper's product ... has ever been used for without sufficient cleaning and/or disinfecting or is being used for the hauling (or back hauling) of garbage ..." — and its meaning cannot be recovered with confidence; it also ends in the catch-all "or other similar items" after a long enumerated list (garbage, trash, hazardous waste, dried animal feed, toxic compound, broken glass, pesticides, fertilizers, petroleum products, solvents, strong aromatic compounds, metal shavings), the classic ejusdem generis scope problem. Paragraphs 11 and 12 are bare fragments — "Single shipment charge." and "Inspection charge." — with no rate, trigger or definition. Paragraph 2 makes cleanliness "the Shipper's sole judgement," an unreviewable standard. Offsetting these, paragraph 5 carefully defines "secure lot" and paragraphs 7–9 set concrete deadlines. On balance just below the flag.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 1 defines "delivery" as transport "to consignee's receiving location from the Shipper's facilities," while § 3(m) defines the same defined term as transport "to consignee's door or job site" — two operative definitions, with § 24 making this Exhibit version control. Paragraph 2 gives Shipper sole judgment on trailer suitability, while § 3(b) provides that Customer's failure to reject a trailer does not relieve Carrier — related but not aligned. Paragraphs 11–12 name charges that Schedule B prices as "No charge" for Item 200; the item's title ("Provisions Included in Base Rates") largely harmonises that. Real seams, below the flag.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 200 – Provisions Included in Base Rates

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single definite rule: mileage is determined by PC Miler 2000, in "the version of which is in effect for Exel at time of tendering." Tying the version to Customer's own installed version at a fixed moment gives Customer unilateral control but is objectively ascertainable, not ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 280 (Out of Route Miles) specifies a different mileage basis for the same purpose — "PC Miler 2000, V16 (Practical Miles)" — a pinned version and a named routing method, whereas this Item floats the version and says nothing about practical versus shortest miles. Item 220 repeats this Item's floating formulation. Since out-of-route miles are measured against "standard route mileage," the two provisions can yield different baselines for the same shipment. A genuine inconsistency in the rating machinery, though small in consequence.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 210 – Rate Base for Mileage Calculation Applications

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite: a $150 flat charge plus linehaul to the point of reconsignment, an express definition of when a shipment is "considered reconsigned" (new destination identified before or after attempted delivery), and a named mileage source. The one term needing definition is expressly supplied.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B renders the linehaul component as "$150 plus $1.25 per mile," which quantifies rather than contradicts this Item. Checked § 5(c), which forbids reconsignment without Customer's prior authorization and defers to "the procedures of Exhibit A" — this Item supplies them. The PC Miler version formulation differs from Item 280's pinned V16, a minor carry-over of the Item 210/280 mismatch.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 220 – Re-consignments and/or Diversion

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Shipments, which cannot be delivered for reasons beyond control of the carrier" is the operative trigger and its boundary is not drawn anywhere — it is narrower than a consignee refusal and broader than force majeure, and § 21's "without human intervention" test does not by its terms apply to Exhibit A. The pricing sentence is also self-referential: the rate is "as published in Schedule B herein, which is in effect on the date the shipment is returned," but this is not a tariff with dated publications. Elevated for the undefined trigger; below the flag because the sense is broadly recoverable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The cross-reference fails on its own terms. This Item points to Schedule B for the applicable rate, but Schedule B's Item 230 row states no rate: "Charge to be based on point of return to point of reconsignment, determined at time of occurrence." So the price for a returned shipment is left to future determination — an open term — while § 6(c) simultaneously provides that the Exhibit A rates "shall be the sole rates ... which Customer will pay" and that "[n]o additional or accessorial charges shall be assessed or paid without the prior approval of Customer." § 5(d) further routes all refused and undelivered shipments to this indeterminate provision. A genuine unresolved gap in the instrument's pricing architecture; I stop just short of flagging because a court would likely fill it with a reasonable-rate term.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 230 – Return of Shipments

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[W]ith a maximum of 5 stops" is genuinely double-edged: it reads either as a cap on the number of additional stops Carrier must make, or as a cap on the number of stops Carrier may charge for (i.e. a $575 ceiling). Nothing in the item resolves which. The rest — $75.00 first additional stop, $125.00 each thereafter, linehaul increased for additional miles — is precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B reproduces the two stop charges but omits the 5-stop limit entirely, so the ambiguity is not resolved by the rate table. Checked § 3(f), under which Carrier will stop in transit to partially load or unload "[a]t Customer's request" with no numerical limit — which cuts against reading the 5 as a service cap. Also checked Item 280: the additional miles from a stop-off are charged here through increased linehaul and there at $1.25 per mile as out-of-route miles, with no stated rule against charging both. Modest overlap.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 240 – Stops in Transit

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One quantified sentence: a $0.10 per-mile surcharge, an identified purpose (a second driver), and a stated condition (expedited service required to meet Shipper's delivery schedule). Nothing open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Matches Schedule B ($0.10 per mile) exactly, and mileage is determined under Item 210. Consistent with § 3(e)'s undertaking to provide short-notice and expedited services. No conflict.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 250 – Expedited Team Service

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite. The right is conditioned on consignor's consent, and the deeming language ("shall be deemed to be for the sole convenience of Carrier") is a clear allocation with a stated consequence — no detention or demurrage charges. The "[n]otwithstanding consignor's consent" opener forecloses the obvious counter-argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked Item 120, which charges detention only "when the Carrier offers a vehicle with a power unit" — drop trailers have no power unit, so the two do not collide. Checked Item 130, which charges storage when Carrier is required to sign for and hold a trailer, i.e. the reverse situation. Schedule B prices Item 260 at "No Charge," consistent with the waiver. Coherent.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 260 – Trailer Placement for Loading

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The charge is expressed as a "$250.00 minimum charge" with no rate basis or ceiling for anything above the minimum, so the text does not say how a larger charge would ever be computed. In practice it functions as a flat $250, and the exceptions (cancellation eight or more hours before pick-up, or another load provided) are precisely stated. Slightly elevated for the dangling "minimum."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B repeats the identical formulation ("$250 minimum charge"), so the instrument is internally consistent even if incomplete. Checked Item 120 (detention) and Item 180 (layover) — both presuppose the truck is used, so no double-charge overlap. Consistent with § 6(c)'s prior-approval regime for accessorials.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 270 – Truck Ordered Not Used

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The item states no rate of its own ("Charge per mile" with the figure omitted) but does supply a precise definition of the thing charged — "any additional miles driven beyond the standard route mileage as calculated using PC Miler 2000, V16 (Practical Miles)" — pinning both the version and the routing method. Definite in substance.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B fills the blank at $1.25 per mile. The real friction is with Item 210, which makes rating mileage turn on "PC Miler 2000, the version of which is in effect for Exel at time of tendering," while this Item pins V16 Practical Miles; the baseline against which out-of-route miles are measured therefore differs from the baseline used to rate the linehaul. Item 220 follows Item 210's floating formulation. Also overlaps Item 240, where extra stop-off miles are recovered through increased linehaul. Genuine but low-value inconsistency.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 280 – Out of Route Miles

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defines "lumper," states the trigger (carrier required to hire a laborer for shipper, consignor or consignee), and sets the measure (actual cost, direct pass-through, receipt to accompany the invoice). Fully determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Matches Schedule B ("Pass through with receipt") and dovetails with § 6(d), which requires Carrier to submit "copies of unloading/lumping receipts, Com-checks/T-checks and the like ... with original Carrier invoice." Item 170 covers carrier personnel rather than hired lumpers, so the two are complementary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "[I]s deemed as the cause for the consignee inability to unload" uses the passive with no decision-maker identified — deemed by whom, and on what showing? In a charge-allocation provision that matters. The item is also purely negative: it says only when redelivery charges do not apply, never when they do or in what amount. Elevated for the unattributed "deemed."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Schedule B supplies the amount ($75 per shipment) that the item omits, so the gap is filled. Checked Item 120, which likewise addresses late or early carrier arrival by excluding the appointment-to-arrival differential from detention time — consistent in principle (Carrier bears its own lateness). Checked § 5(b), requiring immediate notification of delivery problems. No contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Unusually careful for this Exhibit: $25 per day, free time fixed at both origin and destination, the counting rule spelled out (pick-up or notify day plus two free days), and the weekend rule worked through day by day, with the Thursday/Friday and Monday/Tuesday/Wednesday cases stated explicitly and consistently with the "falls within the free time" principle. The only omission is a Saturday or Sunday pick-up, an edge case the general rule still resolves.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Matches Schedule B ($25 per day after expiration of free time). Item 320 expressly adopts this free-time schedule, so the two intermodal items interlock. Its intermodal subject matter is unusual in a motor carrier agreement, but § 3's scope is broad and Item 320 confirms the parties intended intermodal coverage.
judgments.clause_name: Exhibit A, Item 310 – Per Diem - Intermodal Only

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, fully specified: two days' free time, $100.00 per day thereafter, and an express incorporation of Item 310's free-time schedule rather than a fresh and possibly divergent counting rule. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 320 is missing from the Exhibit A SPECIAL SERVICES index, which stops at "Intermodal Per Diem 310," although the charge does appear in Schedule B — an indexing gap rather than a substantive conflict. Checked Item 130 (OTR storage at $40 per day): the two storage rates differ, but Item 130 is expressly limited to OTR shipments and Item 320 to intermodal, so they do not overlap. Checked Item 310, whose free-time schedule this Item adopts by reference — that cross-reference lands. Mildly elevated for the omission from the index.
